title: The Glory Returns to the Temple
summary: At the east gate Ezekiel sees the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east, with a voice like many waters, and it enters and fills the temple. God speaks from within: this is the place of his throne, where he will dwell among Israel forever, and his people must put away the idolatry and defilement that drove him out. Ezekiel is to describe the temple so the people will be ashamed and keep its laws. The chapter ends with the altar's measurements and a seven-day rite to cleanse and consecrate it, after which God will accept his people's offerings.
story: This is the climax of the book. In chapters 10 and 11 Ezekiel watched the glory of the LORD rise from a defiled temple, pause at the east gate, and leave the city toward the mountain on the east. Everything since, the fall of Jerusalem, the promises of a new heart, the dry bones, the defeat of Gog, the measuring of a new temple, has been leading to this moment. Now the glory comes back by the same road, from the east, through the same gate, and fills the house. The God who left has returned. The rest of the vision (chapters 44 to 48) describes the life of the people around his presence, ending with the city's new name, The LORD is there.
historical:
The vision belongs to the unit dated to about 573 BC (40:1), when the temple Ezekiel had known lay in ruins. Verses 7 to 9 recall specific features of the old Jerusalem. Solomon built his palace right beside the temple (1 Kings 7:1-12), so that the royal house and God's house shared a wall, and later kings brought idolatry into the temple courts (2 Kings 21:4-7; 23:11-12). The phrase translated "funeral offerings for their kings" is disputed: the Hebrew word usually means corpses, and interpreters take it as the burial of kings too close to the sanctuary, as memorial monuments to dead kings, or as offerings made for them. In each case the complaint is the same: royal power and its rites had crowded in on God's holy space.

The altar described in verses 13 to 17 is a stepped structure rising in stages from a base, some ten or eleven long cubits high (roughly 5 to 6 meters), with horns at its corners and steps on its east side. Some scholars compare its terraced shape to Mesopotamian temple towers, which Ezekiel would have seen in Babylon; others simply see an enlargement of Israel's own great altars. Its dedication by seven days of sin offerings follows the pattern of Moses' consecration of the tabernacle altar and priests (Exodus 29:36-37; Leviticus 8).
cultural:
In the ancient world a temple was a god's house and throne room, and the arrival of the god's presence, often represented by a statue, was what made a building a temple. Israel had no statue. Instead, the glory of the LORD, the radiant, visible sign of God's presence, filled the tabernacle and Solomon's temple at their dedication (Exodus 40:34-35; 1 Kings 8:10-11). Ezekiel's vision follows that pattern: the building is measured and complete, but it is not a temple until the glory enters.

The east was the direction of sunrise, and in Ezekiel's time people had worshiped the sun at the temple, facing east with their backs to the sanctuary (8:16). In the new temple the altar's steps face east, so the priest going up to it faces west, toward God's house. The altar's horns were projections at its corners where sacrificial blood was applied (Exodus 29:12). The phrase "the place for the soles of My feet" draws on the image of the ark as God's footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 132:7).
literary: The chapter moves from vision to law. Verses 1 to 5 are narrative, and Ezekiel deliberately links this sight to his earlier visions by the Kebar and at the city's destruction (verse 3). Verses 6 to 12 are God's speech from inside the temple, the first time in chapters 40 to 48 that God himself speaks rather than the guide; it frames the whole program with the words "This is the law of the temple" (verse 12, stated twice). Verses 13 to 27 shift to regulations, first architectural (the altar's measurements) and then ritual (the seven-day consecration). The pattern is significant: the presence of God comes first, and the laws of holiness follow as the right response to it.

outline.t: The glory of the LORD returns from the east and fills the temple
God's throne among his people forever
Show the people the design and the law of the temple
The seven-day consecration of the altar

doctrines.note: "This is the place of My throne and the place for the soles of My feet, where I will dwell among the Israelites forever" (verse 7). The goal of the whole book is God's own presence among his people, not only their return to the land.

God's return requires that his people "remove far from Me their prostitution" (verse 9), and the whole mountain around the temple becomes "most holy" (verse 12). Holiness spreads outward from God's presence to everything around it.

Before the altar can be used, blood is applied to cleanse it and "make atonement for it" (verse 20). Access to God depends on sin being dealt with, and only then does God say "I will accept you" (verse 27).
Ezekiel is to describe the temple "so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities" (verse 10). Seeing the beauty of God's design is meant to produce honest shame and a changed life.

words.note: Kavod, glory. The root means heaviness or weight, and the noun names honor, splendor, and in Ezekiel the visible radiance of God's presence. Its departure (chapters 10 and 11) and return (here) are the book's spine.
Shakan, to dwell, to settle. It gives the word mishkan, tabernacle, the dwelling where God lived among Israel in the wilderness. God promises here to dwell among his people forever (verses 7 and 9).

Kipper, to make atonement, to purge or cover. In priestly law it describes cleansing sin and impurity so that the relationship with God can continue. Here even the altar must be atoned for before it can serve.
Torah, instruction, law. "This is the law of the temple" (verse 12). Torah means more than rules; it is God's teaching for how his people are to live in his presence.

christ: John's Gospel says of Jesus, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). The verb John uses is related to the Greek word for tent or tabernacle, recalling the glory that filled Israel's sanctuary, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom God's glory returned to dwell with his people. He spoke of his body as the temple (John 2:19-21). Revelation's voice "like the roar of many waters" belongs to the risen Christ (Revelation 1:15), the same description Ezekiel gives here, and Revelation's closing vision announces that the dwelling place of God is with humanity, and he will dwell with them (Revelation 21:3). The consecration of the altar by blood also stands behind the New Testament's teaching that Christ, by his own blood, has cleansed the way into God's presence once for all (Hebrews 9:11-14).

hard.q: Why does Ezekiel's future temple have animal sacrifices, when the New Testament says Christ's sacrifice ended them?
hard.a: Hebrews teaches that Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and that where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin (Hebrews 10:12, 18). Readers reconcile this with Ezekiel 43 in several ways. Dispensational interpreters who expect a literal millennial temple hold that its sacrifices will not take away sin, which Christ alone does, but will serve as memorials looking back to the cross (as the Lord's Supper does now) or as means of ceremonial purity for a holy place where God's presence dwells among a people who are not yet glorified. Many other Christians read the sacrifices as the prophet describing future worship in the only terms his readers could understand, so that the vision's point, full atonement and acceptance before God, is fulfilled in Christ, the church, and the new creation. Others read chapters 40 to 48 as a program offered to the returning exiles, whose sacrifices belonged to the old covenant still in force at that time. Jewish readers take the sacrifices as part of the worship of a future temple. Christians agree on the first-order point: Christ's death is the full and final atonement for sin. The second-order question is how Ezekiel's vision relates to it.

questions: The glory returns by the same road it left. What does that tell you about God's faithfulness after judgment?
God tells Ezekiel to show the people the temple so they will be ashamed of their sins (verse 10). How can seeing God's goodness lead to repentance more deeply than hearing a list of wrongs?
The kings had built their palace right up against God's house, with only a wall between (verse 8). Where do other loyalties crowd up against God's place in your life?
